# University of Edinburgh
The University of Edinburgh, established in 1583 as Tounis College and later known by its current name in the 17th century, is one of Scotland’s ancient universities with a strong historical footing in the Enlightenment and medical education. It comprises five main campuses: the Central Area (housing arts, humanities, social sciences, informatics, and law), King’s Buildings (science and engineering), BioQuarter (medical facilities), Easter Bush (veterinary studies and animal sciences), and Western General (biomedical research). Notable historic and modern buildings include St Cecilia's Hall, Teviot Row House, Old College, McEwan Hall, and the Roslin Institute, famous for cloning Dolly the sheep.
Governance is constitutionally defined by the Universities (Scotland) Acts, with the University Court as the legal governing body, the General Council representing graduates, and the Senatus Academicus overseeing academic matters. The university is organized into three main Colleges—Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences; Science & Engineering; and Medicine & Veterinary Medicine—with 21 schools offering a wide array of subjects and research disciplines. The Edinburgh Medical School has an eminent global reputation, historically and presently, associated with numerous Nobel laureates. The university also hosts extensive research centers, such as the Centre for Regenerative Medicine and the Edinburgh Cancer Research Centre, and maintains robust student life with active sports traditions, student co-operatives, and regular activism. Financially, Edinburgh reported a total income of £1.386 billion in 2024 and maintains one of the largest university endowments in the UK.
